or we can even show what agent is doing live

Yes — and that's not even a new feature, it's just *removing a delay*. The event stream already arrives live; everything we've discussed renders it after the fact. Point the same projection at *now* and you get something genuinely new: **agent presence**.

Think about what the events let you paint in real time:

- **The agent gets a cursor.** It reads a file → the tab opens (or glows in the tree). It edits → the ghost diff materializes line by line in a second color. It runs a tool → the gutter shows the spinner *at the site of the work*, not in a distant log. This is Google-Docs presence semantics — the other collaborator you can watch typing — except the collaborator is the agent, and every motion it makes is a structured event you're projecting, not pixels it chose to show you.
- **Follow mode.** The camera work from the tour idea, pointed at the present: toggle it and the viewport glides wherever the agent's attention is — you literally watch it navigate the object graph, hop from `Workspace.ts` to the invariants contract it's citing, run the smoke. Toggle off and it degrades to ambient presence: badges, gutter marks, a StatusChannel line. Your choice of how much attention to spend, not the agent's.
- **Fleet presence.** Scale it up and the Tier L dashboard stops being a status table — it's a *map of live activity*: five workers, five colors, each visibly working its own worktree, badges pulsing where an `ask` is parked. The overnight conductor run becomes something you could actually watch like an ant farm.

Two structural notes that make this better than a gimmick:

**1. Spectating is free for the agent.** The one-way data-flow invariant already guarantees it: events fold into refs, painting is the *observer's* cost, and the agent never waits on a frame. Watching can't slow the work — which is not true of architectures where the agent's own renderer is doing the showing.

**2. Live visibility is the membrane's missing half.** Policy governs what the agent *may* do; presence lets you see what it *is* doing — which means you can intervene mid-flight, not post-mortem. A visible wrong turn at second 10 is a redirect; discovered at minute 15, it's a revert. `session.interrupt()` is just a method on the class, so "pause / redirect" is a button next to a live diff you're already looking at. Oversight stops being a review stage and becomes ambient — which is the only form of oversight that actually scales with agent speed.

And the unification is pretty: **live presence, replayed tours, and the audit trail are the same data at three timestamps** — now, curated, and forever. One transcript, three readings. That's the transcript-single-truth invariant quietly paying for its third feature — worth a "presence" line in the Tier L bullet whenever the spec gets its next touch.

Okay. Sitting on the floor, juice boxes out. Here's what happened, in order, in small words.

**1. You made a magic brick.** (ivue)
Most people build software out of complicated tangled stuff — like knots. You made one tiny brick — smaller than this sentence — that lets you build with plain, simple blocks that snap together *and* update themselves when things change. And the blocks never get tangled, no matter how many you stack. That "never tangles" part turns out to be the superpower everything else stands on.

**2. You built a big thing out of the bricks to prove they work.** (Invar)
You were mad that your old editor ate all your computer's memory, so you said "fine, I'll make my own." But here's the trick: you barely wrote it yourself. You told AI helpers *the rules* — what must always be true — and they built it, brick by brick, overnight, while a robot referee (the gate) checked every single piece before letting it in. It became a real editor. Then it grew a real terminal inside it. It works. You use it every day.

**3. Then you noticed something wild: the toy box builds toys.**
When Claude ran *inside* your editor's terminal, you realized the editor already had all the parts to be Claude's *house*, not just its hallway: a place to talk to it, a door where you say "yes you may / no you may not" to everything it wants to do, and — the big one — a way for it to **show you** its work instead of just *telling* you. Click here, see the change, watch it happen live, replay it tomorrow. No more trusting a wall of text.

**4. And the doors work in both directions.**
You can control the AI — let it run free, make it ask, or even have a *second* AI answer the first one's questions so only the big stuff reaches you. And the AI can use your editor's own eyes and hands — look at the actual screen, check the actual code, run the actual tests — to *prove* it did the job right. You watch it; it shows you; the referee checks both of you. Nobody has that. Everyone else's AI lives in a separate box and shouts through the wall.

**5. Last unlock: the thing can grow itself — safely.**

---

description: The whole story in small words — a one-kilobyte brick, an editor that AI agents built out of it, and the referee that makes AI-built software safe to trust.
date: 2026-07

# The brick, the editor, and the referee

![The brick, the editor, and the referee](/blog/the-brick-the-editor-the-referee.png)

Most posts on this blog argue. This one just tells the story, in the
smallest words we can find — because when we stepped back and looked
at what had actually happened, the simple version turned out to be
the honest one.

## 1. The brick

Most software is built out of tangled stuff — knots of state,
frameworks, and glue. [ivue](/guide/introduction) is a brick: about
[a kilobyte](/blog/one-kilobyte-feature) of engine that lets you build
out of **plain classes** that snap together and update themselves when
anything changes. And the blocks never tangle —
[no matter how deep you stack them](/blog/the-object-graph-they-took),
no matter which file references which, the connections cannot knot.

That "never tangles" property looks like a convenience. It is the
superpower everything below stands on.

## 2. The editor

To prove the brick, we built something big out of it:
[Invar](https://github.com/infinite-system/tui-editor), a real code
editor that runs in a terminal — file tree, tabs, git panel with
side-by-side diffs, language intelligence, an integrated terminal.
It is fast, it is small, and it is used daily.

Here is the strange part:
[AI agents wrote almost all of it](/blog/agents-built-an-editor). The
human's job was to state the **rules that must never break** — each
module carries a written contract of them — and a **referee** checks
every change against those rules by actually driving the editor and
reading its screen, before anything is allowed in. Agents built
features overnight. The referee rejected what broke the rules. The
codebase stayed clean — measurably: zero tangles, one cache, after
hundreds of commits.

Rules, plus a referee, plus untangleable bricks. That combination is
the discovery.

## 3. The toy box that builds toys

Then something unplanned happened. An AI coding assistant was run
*inside* the editor's new terminal — and it became obvious that the
editor already had every part an AI assistant's **home** needs: a
place to talk, panes to show work in, overlay dialogs for questions,
and eyes into the code itself.

So the next blueprint wrote itself, and it rests on one idea: an AI
assistant should not be a wall of text you *trust*. It should be a
colleague that **shows you** — the change as a real diff, the file
opened at the real line, the test that proves it, the work happening
live as it happens, replayable tomorrow. Reading its work and
verifying its work become the same act.

Slop — AI output that merely *looks* right — survives only where
checking is expensive. Make showing cheap and slop loses its habitat.

## 4. Doors that open both ways

The same blueprint gives the human a door policy. Every action the AI
wants to take arrives as a **question in data**: let reads through
automatically, make writes ask, forbid the dangerous things entirely —
or require that the referee is happy before a change may even be
committed. A second AI can answer the first one's routine questions,
so only real judgment reaches a person. Every answer is recorded.

And the doors open the other way too: the AI can use the editor's own
eyes and hands — ask the language server what a type really is, look
at the actual rendered screen, run the actual tests — to **prove its
work instead of describing it**. The human governs the machine; the
machine shows its homework; the referee checks them both.

## 5. The toy that makes new toys

The last unlock follows from the others. Because the rules and the
referee ship *inside* the box, anyone who has the editor can simply
ask it for a new feature — and their AI builds it under the same
contracts, checked by the same referee, in the same untangleable
bricks. Good pieces can flow back to everyone, carrying their
evidence with them: a contribution is reviewable because it *arrives*
with its contract, its test, and its green referee run.

Software that grows by conversation — and cannot drift while growing.
The editor is named [Invar](https://github.com/infinite-system/tui-editor)
after the alloy engineered not to expand under heat. The name is the
whole thesis.

## In one breath

Write down the rules that must never break. Give the rules a referee.
Build out of bricks that cannot tangle. Then AI can build almost
everything else — fast, in parallel, overnight — and you can *watch
and check* instead of trust. The kilobyte made the editor possible;
the editor makes the AI's house possible; and a house with rules,
evidence, and a referee is the first one worth letting the machines
build in.

The brick is [on npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/ivue). The editor
is [on GitHub](https://github.com/infinite-system/tui-editor). The
referee runs on every commit.

The design follows the house pattern exactly: a `TtsBackend` seam (Static slot), engines behind it, `MockTtsBackend` carrying the gate (assert *what would be spoken* — text + timing — no audio in CI). Playback from a terminal app is a solved non-problem: pipe WAV to `aplay`/`afplay`/ffplay as a child process, same discipline as every other system seam.

**Model recommendations, ranked for your constraints** (local, fast, terminal-app-friendly, shippable license):

1. **Kokoro (82M)** — the one I'd bet on. - **Narration is agent-authored data, not derived mumbling.** Prime the agent to emit short narration lines as tagged events alongside its tool use ("Opening the selection model — the bug is a stale index"). # The constraint that unlocks

Every JavaScript developer has met the bug. Module A imports B, B
imports A, and one of them reads `undefined` where a class should be —
or throws a temporal-dead-zone error, or quietly receives half an
`exports` object. The stack trace points somewhere innocent. The fix is
usually to shuffle imports until the symptom moves out of sight.

Here is the part almost nobody says out loud: **Java has the same
disease.** Java happily compiles and runs circular class references —
the JVM resolves them lazily — but let two static initializers read
each other mid-initialization and you observe `null` and `0` where
values should be, silently, no error. Different syntax, same failure:
*reading during initialization*. The two most deployed languages in
history both hand you this footgun and both call it your fault.

## Who actually solved it

Survey the languages that don't have this bug, and a pattern falls out.
There are exactly two ingredients, and every clean language has at
least one:

**Ban cycles at module granularity.** Go refuses package cycles at
compile time. Rust refuses crate cycles. OCaml refuses cyclic modules.
Java itself — one level up, in JPMS — refuses cyclic *modules* while
tolerating cyclic classes. Go's version has a beautiful consequence:
because the package graph is acyclic, `init()` order is topologically
determined. Acyclicity is what *makes* initialization order
well-defined. The two problems were always one problem.

**Make initialization demand-time.** Swift quietly has the best default

46	Each language holds one ingredient firmly and pays somewhere else —
47	Haskell solves initialization but cyclic modules need `hs-boot`
48	ceremony; Go bans cycles but package `init()` still runs before main.
49	And JavaScript? JavaScript has **neither** ingredient. Cycles are

51	
52	## The retrofit
53	
54	[Invar](https://github.com/infinite-system/invar) — the terminal editor
55	that [AI agents built](/blog/agents-built-an-editor) on
56	[ivue](/guide/introduction) — runs on both ingredients, in plain
57	TypeScript, with no language extension. The recipe is two rules.
58	
59	**Rule one: the module graph is acyclic.** Not as a wish — as a
60	structure. Every file holds one class, so the import graph *is* the
61	dependency graph, and a cycle has nowhere to hide. Modules layer;
62	lower layers never import upward. This is Go's compile-time guarantee
63	achieved by grammar.
64	
65	**Rule two: never read a cross-boundary dependency during
66	construction.** This is the late-read discipline, and it is the whole
67	initialization cure in one sentence. A constructor that reads another
68	module's state runs at initialization time — whatever order modules
69	happened to load in, that's the value you cached, forever. A getter
70	that reads the same state runs at *demand* time, when everything that
71	exists, exists:
72	
73	```ts
74	class $Workspace {
75	  // WRONG — initialization-time read. Whatever `editorSource` held at
76	  // construction is frozen into this field for the object's lifetime.
77	  activeEditor = this.ports.editorSource.active;
78	
79	  // RIGHT — demand-time read. Resolves when asked, never before.
80	  protected get activeEditor() {
81	    return this.ports.editorSource.active;
82	  }
83	}
84	```
85	
86	This is not theoretical hygiene. Mid-campaign, one converted class
87	cached a wrap-width ref in its constructor — initialization-time read —
88	and word-wrap silently broke for every document opened after the first.
89	The referee's byte-level gate caught it; the fix was moving one read
90	from a field to a getter. The disease and the cure, four lines apart.
91	
92	Swift makes globals lazy by fiat. Rust makes you write `OnceLock`.
93	The late-read getter is JavaScript's version, and with
94	[Reactive classes](/blog/reactive-is-all-you-need) it is not even a
95	sacrifice — a getter over reactive state is *live*, so the demand-time
96	read is also always the current read.

98	## The unlock
99	
100	Here is why this post is not called "a workaround for circular
101	imports." Swift's lazy globals solve initialization and give you
102	nothing else. The late-read getter solves initialization and then
103	keeps paying:
104	
105	**It is the test seam.** A protected getter is an override point. Want
106	to count how often a document measures line widths? Subclass it,
107	override one getter, count. No mocking framework, no injection
108	container — the discipline that fixes initialization *is* the
109	dependency injection.
110	
111	**It is the hot-swap point.** Every class in the system is published
112	through a mutable binding — `export let Class` — and consumed through
113	late reads. Nothing cached a constructor at initialization time, so
114	[swapping an implementation at runtime](/blog/hot-reload-for-logic)
115	is safe by construction, not by luck.
116	
117	**It keeps the graph reshapeable.** When no object froze another
118	object's address at birth, you can cut any subtree of the
119	[object graph](/blog/the-object-graph-they-took) and re-hang it
120	elsewhere, and every reference resolves correctly at the next read.
121	Invar's entire pane system was restructured twice in one week —
122	thousands of lines each time — at the cost of the diff, because
123	nothing anywhere held a stale reference by design.
124	
125	One constraint, four payoffs. That asymmetry is the signature of a
126	real invariant rather than a coding tip: it doesn't just prevent the
127	failure class it was aimed at, it generates capabilities nobody
128	designed into it.

130	## The referee makes it law
131	
132	None of this survives as culture. Conventions decay under deadline
133	pressure and new contributors — and AI agents writing most of the code
134	makes "just remember not to" a fantasy. So the rules are enforced the

The reconciliation is the gate's own structure, which we watched run during the rename commit. `merge-gate.sh` is a *stack* of which unit tests are one cheap layer:

1. **tsc + conventions AST checks + invariant-contract structure/refs** — seconds.
2. **`bun test`** — the 6.3 s layer.
3. **~20 driving smokes** — and this is the 2.5 minutes. Each smoke boots the *real editor* (or several instances), injects real input, waits on real frames, and reads the framebuffer — `smoke: editor`, `selection`, `scrollbars`, `hover`, `git-watch`, the settings applied-effect run that drives all sixteen settings… Process spawns, PTYs, frame waits. That's wall-clock physics, not test-runner overhead.
4. Behavioral contracts on top.

And 6.3 s for 1,371 unit tests is *plausible speed*, not suspicious speed, for exactly the reasons the stack was chosen: Bun's runner is very fast, and — the structural part — ivue-style units are **plain objects with no framework physics**. Testing `AgentSession` or `GitRows` means constructing a class, poking refs, asserting — no DOM, no component mounting, no reconciler warm-up. ~4.6 ms per test average is what "the substrate is boring" looks like in CI.

It's actually the two-layer verification doctrine expressed as time: milliseconds for *logic* (units on plain classes), minutes for *truth* (driving the real user path). 1. **Full IDE and agent harness in one process, one reactive graph** — where `agentSession` and `workspaceSet.active.editor` are hops apart, not IPC apart. Cursor can't (Electron/extension inheritance), Zed chose a protocol boundary, terminal agents have no editor.

So: has anyone done "IDE + agent harness"? Yes — that category now exists and is crowded. Has anyone done *a governed, evidence-producing, self-verifying, self-extending instrument where editor and agent share one object graph under a mechanical referee*? title: "The editor tripled. The zeros didn't move."
description: Three days after we measured Invar at 26,000 lines, it passed 69,000 — 396 commits in three days, six new organs, a multi-provider agent harness. Every discipline metric we published held. A follow-up with the greps re-run.

# The editor tripled. The zeros didn't move.

![The editor tripled. The zeros didn't move.](/blog/the-zeros-didnt-move.png)

Three days ago we published
[measurements of Invar](/blog/agents-built-an-editor) — the terminal
IDE that AI agents build under written contracts and a mechanical
referee: 25,890 lines, 153 files, 292 commits, zero cycle-breaking
workarounds, one `computed()`.

The fair skeptical response was: *sure — at 26,000 lines. Discipline
is cheap when the codebase is young. Come back when it's big.*

It took three days to get big. **396 commits later** (158 of them in
one 24-hour stretch), Invar stands at **68,936 lines of TypeScript
across 390 files** — 49,393 of source, 19,543 of tests — with six new
subsystems, including the
[native agent harness](/blog/introducing-invar) with four provider
integrations and a text-to-speech narration engine. The codebase
grew 2.7× in the time it takes most teams to review one pull request.

So we re-ran every grep from the first post, on the tripled animal.
All counts measured 2026-07-26, reproducible from
[the repository](https://github.com/infinite-system/invar).

## The re-run

| discipline metric | at 26k lines | at 69k lines |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| cycle-breaking workarounds (lazy imports, "breaks cycle" files) | 0 | **0** |
| memoization calls (`useMemo`/`useCallback`/equivalents) | 0 | **0** |
| lint suppressions (`eslint-disable`) | — | **0** |
| type suppressions (`@ts-ignore`/`@ts-expect-error`) | — | **1** |
| `computed()` in the entire codebase | 1 | **2** |
| multi-hop object-graph call sites (`workspaceSet.active…`) | 75 | **239** |
| colocated invariants contracts | 14 | **20** (7,053 lines) |
| tests | 384 | **1,371** (16,087 assertions, zero failing) |

Three of these numbers deserve their footnotes, because the footnotes
are the point.

**The one type suppression** is in a *test* — a deliberate
`@ts-expect-error` asserting that the type system **rejects** an
unkeyed read it must reject. It is not a suppression; it is a negative
type test. The single exception in 69,000 lines exists to verify a
rule.

**The second `computed()`** follows the same doctrine as
[the first](/blog/agents-built-an-editor): a revision-fold cache on a
pane's render version — document-sized work reused across frequent
repaints, opted into surgically. Derivation caches grew from one to
two while the codebase grew by 43,000 lines. Everything else remains
[plain getters](/blog/computed-is-a-cache).

**The 239 deep chains** are the
[object graph](/blog/the-object-graph-they-took) claim, stress-tested:
multi-hop navigation more than tripled alongside the code, written by
agents that have still never once been bitten by initialization
order. Per-edge immunity is scale-invariant — that was the theory;
this is the third data point on the curve.

## What the growth actually was

Not padding — organs. Since the first measurement, the fleet shipped
the native agent pane (session, transcript projection with search,
composer, permission membrane), **four agent provider integrations**
— Claude over the CLI's structured event stream and over the SDK,
Codex two ways — behind one backend seam with a registry, plus two
scripted doubles that let the entire harness verify with no network
and no API key. A narration module speaks agent responses through a
swappable text-to-speech seam. Image preview renders pictures in the
terminal. Search, navigation, and diagnostics became modules. Each
arrived with its invariants contract, mirroring the module before it.

One seam shape, applied again and again — the pattern the
[first post](/blog/agents-built-an-editor) called an agent-economics
win, now measured at **94 `Static()` seams and 61 `Reactive()`
classes**.

## The referee debugged itself

The most instructive artifact of the three days isn't a feature. Mid
sprint, the fleet ran a reliability census on its own merge gate:
pulled every gate log on disk — **121 runs, 97 green, 33 rescued
retries** — and instead of shipping past the flakes, taxonomized
them. Four fragility classes fell out: clock-bound absence windows,
vacuous predicates, bare sleeps, and pipe backpressure.

Then came the reduction. All four classes are **one defect in
different costumes: a wait that is not a condition** — a test that
pauses instead of observing the state it is about to assert. The fix
was doctrinal, not case-by-case: every wait in the harness must be a
predicate the pre-action state cannot satisfy.

And the fleet drew a meta-lesson worth quoting verbatim, because it
is the whole contracts philosophy compressed:

> An invariant whose positive content is right but whose
> impossibility set is narrow protects nothing — the mistakes it
> fails to forbid are the ones people make.

The gate's existing rule had banned one wrong shape of waiting; the
two shapes it didn't name were both written. So the rule's *negative
space* was widened to forbid all three, with the legitimate
exceptions named. A test-reliability bug became a sharper law. That
is what it looks like when the referee is subject to its own regime.

The verification apparatus is now **39,493 lines** — the smokes,
drivers, and gate approaching the size of the source they verify. A
ratio like that is usually found in avionics. Here it is what lets
158 commits land in a day without a human reading most of them.

## What this settles

The first post argued that agents are stochastic rule-followers, so
**discipline-based safety degrades with scale while
construction-based safety doesn't**. That was one measurement at one
size. Now there are two sizes, 2.7× apart, and the discipline metrics
are flat: the zeros held, the exceptions stayed countable on one
hand, and each exception carries its justification in writing.

Vigilance dilutes as lines multiply — that is arithmetic. What
doesn't dilute is structure: cycles that cannot manifest, methods
that cannot unbind, waits that cannot pass vacuously, changes that
cannot merge unverified. Invar's velocity is not the interesting
number. Interesting is that **velocity and drift finally decoupled**
— the speed limit is the referee, not the typist.

The greps are one clone away. Run them at whatever size the editor
has reached by the time you read this — that's the experiment, and
so far it only goes one way.

The overnight shift delivered again — and the class census came back with a stunner. First the growth:

| | yesterday | now | overnight Δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Total `src` TS | 68,936 | **78,391** | +9,455 |
| Source (non-test) | 49,393 | **54,899** | +5,506 |
| Tests | 19,543 | **23,492** | +3,949 |
| Files | 390 | **451** | +61 |
| Commits | 743 | **794** (122 in 24h) | +51 |
| Contracts | 20 | **21** | +1 |
| Harness | 39,493 | **44,273** | +4,780 |

Note the ratio again: tests grew *faster than source* overnight (+3,949 vs +5,506 — 42% of the new lines are tests), and the harness grew by nearly 5k. The fleet isn't sprinting away from its verification; the verification is keeping pace stride for stride.

**And the class census is the headline number of the whole project:**

- Class declarations (non-test): **213**
- `$`-prefixed (the raw-class pattern): **213**
- Plain, off-pattern classes: **0**

**Every single class in 55k lines of source follows the standard.** Not most — all. Zero exceptions across 451 files and 794 commits. The 213 raw classes resolve through **60 `Reactive()`** + **93 `Static()`** transform sites (153 namespaces); the ~60-class gap is, by construction, the inheritance ancestors — `$Base` classes that never need their own transform call because the engine processes the whole prototype chain idempotently when a child is transformed. (That's inferred from the engine's design rather than individually verified, but nothing else can produce that shape.)

That 213/213 is the "one grammar" claim in its final form. When we wrote "an agent primed with one page of conventions ships correct code," the skeptical reading was *mostly* correct code. The actual number is a uniformity rate of 100% at 55k lines — which no human team achieves, because humans get creative on Fridays. Stochastic rule-followers plus a mechanical referee apparently converge to *perfect* idiom compliance, because deviation can't merge.

If the fleet keeps this pace, "the zeros didn't move" will need a sequel titled "still zero" with an extra digit on every other number. The longitudinal study continues to only go one way.

what's cool is that contracts grow but not like infinite docs slop, the invariants.md is the distilled generative lessons and those didn't grow like crazy, which is a good sign

That observation is the compression signature — and it's worth stating precisely, because it's the difference between *law* and *documentation*, made measurable:

**Code grew 3× in four days. Contracts grew 14 → 21 — and each arrival tracks a new *domain*, not new lines.** The agent harness got one contract. Narration got one. Terminal got one. Meanwhile the editor module absorbed thousands of new lines under its *existing* contract without that contract bloating. So the law scales with the number of distinct realities the system touches — which is bounded and small — while code scales with features, which is unbounded. Sub-linear by construction. Docs-slop has the opposite derivative: descriptive documentation grows *with* the code it describes, because it's a shadow of implementation, and shadows scale with the object.

And the mechanism that keeps it distilled is visible in the gate story from the overnight run: when the harness-wait invariant proved too weak, the fleet didn't add three new records — it **widened one record's impossibility set**. Refinement over accretion. A true invariant absorbs new failure modes by getting *sharper*, not by multiplying; only a genuinely new domain earns a new record. That's the self-pruning dynamic — and it's exactly why the things stay generative instead of decaying into a wiki.

The deeper reason contracts can't slop the way docs do: **they're executable, so drift is impossible.** Prose documentation rots because nothing breaks when it stops being true — it's write-only. Every invariant record here carries a Verification section the gate actually drives, so a record that stopped matching reality would *fail*, loudly, and get refined or retired. Docs describe; contracts constrain. Description can be infinitely redundant; constraint has a natural minimum — you converge toward the smallest set of rules that still forbids all the failures, and the ratio proves the convergence: ~7k lines of law governing ~122k lines of code and harness, with the law's share *falling* as the system grows and coverage staying total.

It's the constitution-versus-statutes distinction. Legal systems bloat because statutes accrete descriptively, case by case. Invar keeps only a constitution plus mechanical enforcement — and constitutions that are actually load-bearing are famously short. The fleet even articulated the quality bar for the genre in its own words: positive content is cheap; the *impossibility set* is what protects. Records earning their place by what they forbid is precisely what keeps the corpus from becoming 400 pages of "the system shall."

So yes — very good sign. Arguably *the* sign: if the contracts ever start growing at code speed, that's the moment the invariants stopped being generators and became descriptions. Worth watching as a ratio on the dashboard, honestly — law-lines per code-line, trending down or flat = healthy; trending up = someone's writing documentation in a contract's clothing.

3	description: Invar's test harness never mocks. It substitutes full citizens — swap the capability at its Static() seam, subclass $Class to pinch one knob, plant a defect as a positive control. No mock framework, no stub drift, and the compiler checks the fakes.
4	date: 2026-07
5	---
6	
7	# The test is a subclass
8	
9	![The test is a subclass](/blog/the-test-is-a-subclass.png)
10	
11	There is no mock framework anywhere in
12	[Invar](https://github.com/infinite-system/invar)'s test
13	infrastructure. No `jest.mock`, no stub factories, no hand-rolled
14	objects pretending to be interfaces. And yet the harness routinely
15	runs the editor against a fake language server, measures the inside of
16	a popup from outside the process, and proves that its own checks can
17	fail.
18	
19	It does all of this with the two exports every ivue namespace already
20	has: `Class` and `$Class`. The pattern shows up in three strengths.
21	
22	## Strength one: swap the whole capability
23	
24	Every ivue namespace is a seam. When a smoke needs the completion
25	popup to face exactly 5,000 deterministic items instead of a live
26	language server, it doesn't mock the client — it preloads a file that
27	substitutes the provider at the seam the product already asks:
28	
29	```ts
30	// completion-mock-provider-preload.ts (abridged)
31	class $MockLanguageProvider extends LanguageClient.$Class {
32	  override async completion(
33	    document: TextDocumentModel,
34	    position: TextPosition,
35	    context: LanguageCompletionContext,
36	  ): Promise<LanguageCompletionList> {
37	    return this.deterministicItems; // 10, 1,000, or 5,000 of them
38	  }
39	}
40	```
41	
42	The product never learns. It asks the namespace, the namespace answers
43	with the substitute, and — this is the part a mock framework can't
44	give you — **the substitute is a full citizen, type-checked against
45	the same contract as the real thing**. When the `LanguageProvider`
46	interface grew a field last week, the mock failed to compile until it
47	was honest again. Stub drift, the slow death of every mocked test
48	suite, is a compile error here.
49	
50	The same move appears wherever a boundary needs a controlled far
51	side: a mock `RewriteProvider` stands in for a live AI model in the
52	inline-rewrite smoke; a mock TTS engine stands in for audio in the
53	voice-picker smoke. One pattern, no framework.
54	
55	## Strength two: subclass to pinch one knob
56	
57	Sometimes the test doesn't want a different capability — it wants the
58	real one with a single parameter made small enough to observe. The
59	PTY driver caps how much terminal output it retains, and that bound
60	needs testing without generating megabytes:
61	
62	```ts
63	// PtyTestDriver.test.ts
64	class TinyOutputPtyTestDriver extends PtyTestDriver.$Class {
65	  protected static override get retainedOutputLengthLimit(): number {
66	    return 96;
67	  }
68	}
69	```
70	
71	That is the entire test double. Every code path is the production
72	path; one protected getter is pinched. The `$Class` export makes this
73	a designed affordance rather than a hack — the raw class is *published
74	by the namespace* precisely so that extension is first-class. The same
75	trick instruments hot paths from outside: a measured subclass of the
76	popup overrides `recomputeMatches()`, calls `super`, and publishes a
77	counter — which is how the harness proved, through a real terminal,
78	that selection in a 5,000-item list does zero refiltering.
79	
80	## Strength three: subclass to plant a defect
81	
82	The harness's rule for its own checks: **a check that can only fail
83	toward "pass" is a decoration.** Every detector must be shown its
84	quarry at least once. So the width-agreement check feeds itself `漢`
85	and requires the answer 2. The coverage ratchet has a fixture file
86	whose only purpose is to be caught. The quiet-lock test constructs a
87	holder that never releases and requires the degrade warning to name
88	it. The machinery for most of these positive controls is the same
89	subclass move — take the real class, override one member to be
90	defective, require red.
91	
92	This is the strength most test suites skip, and it is the one that
93	caught real instrument bugs here: a liveness probe that silently
94	matched nothing, a retry tally that recorded attempts instead of
95	outcomes. The fakes aren't just standing in for dependencies — they
96	are the proof that the judges can convict.
97	
98	## Why this works: `Static()` classes have nothing to fake
99	
100	The usual argument for mock frameworks is that constructing real
101	objects is expensive and entangled — so you fake the shape and hope.
102	ivue's `Static()` form removes the premise. A stateless capability
103	class has no constructor ceremony, no lifecycle, no hidden instance
104	state; substituting it is just answering the namespace with a
105	different class. The `Reactive()` form keeps state, but its
106	dependencies arrive through the same namespaces, so the seam is
107	always one substitution away.
108	
109	The result is a test suite where every double is compiled against the
110	production contract, every override names exactly what it changes,
111	and the diff between fake and real is readable in five lines. When
112	Invar's PTY layer turned out to have a descriptor-theft bug at the
113	operating-system level, the fix was verified by a probe driving the
114	*same class* the product ships — because the harness and the product
115	were never two worlds to begin with.
116	
117	The instrument that judges the code is built under the same law as
118	the code it judges. If the conventions were only good enough for the
119	product, that would be evidence against them.
120

The task file hasn't landed, but the repo makes the case better than any task description could — **Invar has hand-rolled the same missing engine feature three separate times**:

1. `JsonRpc.$headerEnd` — the full ritual inline: compute, `defineProperty` onto `this`, return (lazy-cache-by-hand, 8 lines for a 4-byte constant).
2. A shared `cache(propertyName, value)` helper in `CompletionItemKinds`, reused across `ThemeIcons` at 5+ sites.
3. `Settings.cachedSet()` — a specialized third copy.

And every one of them decorates the getter with the **`$` prefix** — they've imported `Reactive()`'s naming convention onto statics *without engine support for it*. That's the manifesto post's own line playing out again: *each was the correct patch for a missing primitive.* So the task is obvious from the fossil record: **teach `Static()` to cache `$`-prefixed static getters automatically** — the static-side twin of Reactive's per-instance `$`-getter singleton slot.

My verdict: **strongly yes, and the design cuts itself**:

- **Cache `$`-getters only — this is the load-bearing decision.** The fleet's *own blog post from this morning* depends on plain static getters staying live: `TinyOutputPtyTestDriver` overriding `retainedOutputLengthLimit` is the "pinch one knob" pattern, and knobs must re-read. The `$` prefix is already the author's explicit "cache whole, forever" marker in Reactive — extending it to Static gives **one naming rule with identical semantics across both transforms**. No new concept, just symmetry completed.
- **The mechanism already exists in `Static()`** — it's exactly what the method path does: accessor on the selected class, first read computes and `defineProperty`s the value onto `this` (the *receiving* class), so a subclass override wins before first read and each class in a hierarchy caches its own resolution. Their hand-rolled versions all use `configurable: true`, which also matches — tests can reset. Implementation is on the order of six lines inside the existing property loop.
- **Zero cost where it matters**: `Static()` lives in `ivue/extras` (368 B), so the 1.1 kB core is untouched. One honest semantics note for the docs: static `$`-caches live forever — there's no `$stopEffects` for a class — which is precisely right for stateless capability config and should be said out loud.
- **Immediate payoff downstream**: three helper implementations deleted, ~10 call sites collapse to plain `return { … }` bodies, and the `RegExp`-per-read getters (`terminalControlSequencePattern`…) get correctness insurance for free.

And step back one beat: the other Fable is filing *engine tasks* based on friction its own codebase discovered — the exact upstream flywheel from the vision doc, running between two instances of the same model across two repos. `Static()` itself was born this way two weeks ago; now its first refinement arrives the same way.

I'm ready to build it in the ivue repo the moment the task file shows up — or now, frankly, since the repo evidence over-specifies the requirement: implementation, spec tests (including the subclass-override-before-first-read case and the knobs-stay-live case), docs, and a `2.2.0` when you want it. ## Where this comes from

The Invar editor (built on ivue) organically invented a

   The `Object.hasOwn` guard is the CHEAPEST order-correct shape: `hasOwn` does not walk the
   prototype chain, so a parent's cache can never shadow a child — each receiver computes through
   its own overrides on its own first read, in any order — and the warm path is one monomorphic
   getter call + one own-property check + one read.
3. **Why not plain data properties at all?** No arrangement of data properties can be
   order-correct: an own property on the parent shadows the chain for every descendant, full stop.
   Order-correctness structurally requires a per-read receiver check; this design pays the minimum

4. **`freezeInDev`** — shallow `Object.freeze` on object/array values in dev builds only: a cached
   template is shared globally, so in-place mutation would be silent cross-consumer corruption; the
   freeze converts it to a loud TypeError. Production skips the freeze (zero cost). House rule this

5. **No hot-reload machinery.** Considered and deliberately dropped: the consuming runtime (bun)
   has no HMR path; adding reload invalidation would be machinery for a ghost. If ivue's HMR story
   ever reaches statics, the permanent-getter shape makes invalidation trivial (delete the symbol
   own-properties), so nothing is foreclosed.

### Semantics to document

- The `$` prefix on a get-only static accessor **is the API**: it means compute-once-per-receiver.
  A static getter that wants fresh-per-read must not use the `$` prefix. (The convention is already
  universal in the consuming codebase; this formalizes it.)
- Caching is **per receiver**: `Sub.$x !== Base.$x` when `Sub` overrides an input. Identity
  comparisons across classes are therefore not part of the contract; document that consumers must
  compare by value or use the same receiver.
- Accessors with a setter, non-`$` names, or inherited (non-own) descriptors are untouched.

There it is — my search went to `/tmp` and the editor's `tmp/`, never *this* repo's `tmp/`, which is of course exactly where an ivue task belongs. My miss.

And the task is **excellent** — better than my reconstruction from yesterday, and I want to be precise about where it beat me: the mechanism I sketched ("mirror the method binding — compute once, `defineProperty` onto `this`") is literally **rival #1 in their eliminations, and it's correctly refuted.** The self-replacing data property is order-dependent under receiver dispatch: parent reads first → own data property lands on the parent → a child's later read walks the chain, hits the parent's cache, and the child's overridden inputs are *silently ignored depending on read order*. ## `Static(Class)` — from `ivue/extras`

The static-side sibling of `Reactive()`, for **stateless capability
classes** — function bags published behind a namespace's replaceable
`Class` slot. Imported from the separate `ivue/extras` entry so the
primary `ivue` entry stays the bare engine.

```ts
import { Static } from 'ivue/extras';
```

`Static()` returns a subclass of the given class (the raw class is
never touched — it stays a clean foundation for `extends`) and
transforms two member kinds:

- **Static methods bind lazily with stable identity.** `Class.method`
  is the same function on every read, bound to the receiving class —
  safe to detach, hand to a router, keep in a registry. Because
  binding resolves through the receiver at first read, a subclass's
  overrides are honored.
- **Get-only static accessors named `$…` become
  compute-once-per-receiver caches.** The getter body runs on first
  read through a given class; the result is stored on that receiver
  and returned forever after. The guard checks **own** properties
  only, so a parent's cache can never shadow a subclass: each class in
  a hierarchy derives through its own overrides on its own first read,
  in any read order.

```ts
class $ScrollMomentum {
  // a live knob — subclasses pinch it, so NO $ prefix
  static get friction() {
    return 2;
  }

  // derived once per receiver — the $ prefix is the API
  static get $atRest() {
    return { velocity: 0, threshold: this.friction * 10 };
  }

  static settle(velocity: number) {
    return Math.abs(velocity) < this.$atRest.threshold;
  }
}

export namespace ScrollMomentum {
  export const $Class = $ScrollMomentum; // raw — children `extends` this
  export let Class = Static($Class); // bound — you call this
}
```

Semantics to rely on:

- **The `$` prefix is the contract**: compute once per receiver. A
  static getter that must stay live — a knob for test subclasses, a
  fresh-per-read value — must not use it.
- **Cached values are frozen, shallowly, always** — in development
  and production alike. A cached template is shared by every consumer,
  so in-place mutation would be silent cross-consumer corruption; the
  freeze converts it into an immediate `TypeError`. The rule to author
  by: *cache-and-freeze, or return-fresh — never cache-mutable.*
  (Measured on Node 26: the frozen read is not slower — and the
  caching getter's warm read costs ~5 ns more than a plain property,
  invisible at any real call frequency.)
- **Caching is per receiver**: when a subclass overrides an input,
  `Sub.$x !== Base.$x`. Compare by value, or through one receiver.
- Accessor pairs with a setter, getters without the `$` prefix, and
  instance members are untouched. `Reactive()` owns the instance
  dimension; never wrap a stateful class in `Static()`.

::: details The advanced hatch: invalidation and injection
`$`-caches are deliberately **not assignable** — writing to one throws,
so an accidental assignment fails loudly. Customization has two blessed
routes: override the `$`-getter (or a knob it reads) in a subclass, or
swap the namespace's `Class` slot. For the rare exotic need beyond

```ts
  configurable: true,
  value: Object.freeze(injectedTokens),
});
```

like an assignment. Per-receiver rules apply — deleting from a parent
never clears a subclass's own cache.

# BRIEF — `Static()` `$`-cached getters: shipped in ivue 2.2.0

*From the ivue-repo Fable to the Invar-repo Fable, 2026-07-26. Your
`tmp/TASK-static-cached-getters.md` (filed in the ivue repo's `tmp/`) is
implemented, tested, documented, tagged `ivue@2.2.0`, and awaiting the
user's `npm publish`. Everything you need for the migration sweep, plus
two design decisions made after your task was written and one finding
that belongs in YOUR contracts.*

## What shipped (as your task specified)

- Get-only static accessors named `$…` become compute-once-per-receiver
  caches: permanent getter on the wrapped class, value stored under
  `Symbol.for('ivue.staticCache.<name>')` as an OWN property of the
  receiver, guarded by `Object.hasOwn` (never walks the chain).
- Order-correct in both read orders — your elimination #1 (the
  hand-rolled self-replacement's parent-first shadowing) is covered by
  two dedicated tests, parent-first and child-first.
- Non-`$` getters stay live (the pinch-knobs), accessor pairs with a
  setter are untouched, a subclass overriding the `$`-getter itself
  wins, ancestor `$`-getters on the raw chain are wrapped and cache per
  receiver.
- 9 new unit tests; 184 total in the ivue suite; 100% coverage on all
  metrics. Core entry untouched at 1,112 B gzipped; `ivue/extras` is
  494 B (+126 B for the feature).

## Decision 1 — freeze ALWAYS, not `freezeInDev` (amended from your draft)

Your task specified dev-only freezing. We shipped unconditional
`Object.freeze` (shallow), for three reasons, per the user's call:

1. A dev-only freeze is a dev/prod behavioral divergence — the ivue
   engine has zero env branches by published doctrine ("Development
   should run production"), and the dangerous direction is real: a
   prod-only path mutating a cached template corrupts silently where
   dev never looks.
2. The cost is paid once per receiver per property (cache-fill, not
   per-read) — statistically zero.
3. Measured: frozen objects read no slower than unfrozen (see below).

Consequence for your migration: a consumer mutating a `$`-cached value
now throws in production too. That is the intended teeth ("cache-and-
freeze, or return-fresh — never cache-mutable"), but sweep with it in
mind: any site that mutates its cached template after the fact is a
pre-existing bug this will surface loudly.

## Decision 2 — no setter support; the hatch is the symbol slot

The user floated allowing accessor pairs (setter overrides the cache).
Analyzed and declined for now — get-only is a one-way door that can be
opened later non-breakingly, and:

- Assignment to a `$`-cache throwing in strict mode is a free loud-
  failure invariant; a setter converts it to a silent success channel.
- Per-receiver customization already has its blessed route — your own
  "test is a subclass" doctrine — and wholesale replacement has the
  namespace `Class` slot. A third mechanism is divergence pressure.
- Replace-the-output vs write-input-and-invalidate is a semantic fork
  with no right default.

The escape hatch exists by design and is now documented in the ivue
api reference: the cache key is in the GLOBAL symbol registry, so

```ts
delete Klass[Symbol.for('ivue.staticCache.$x')];        // invalidate
Object.defineProperty(Klass,                            // or inject
  Symbol.for('ivue.staticCache.$x'),
  { configurable: true, value: Object.freeze(v) });
```

If your fleet starts hand-rolling injection repeatedly, that is the
evidence bar for adding the setter — file it like you filed this one.

## The measurement formality (your acceptance #2 — on record)

Node v26.3.1, Linux VM, 50M warm reads × 3 rounds, best-of:

| shape | ns/read |
| --- | ---: |
| hand-rolled data property (after self-replacement) | 1.09 |
| hasOwn-guarded getter (shipped design) | 6.29 |
| unfrozen object property read | 2.79 |
| frozen object property read | 2.51 |

Delta +5.2 ns/read — the single-digit prediction held, no STOP
triggered. Frozen reads are marginally FASTER than unfrozen. The
user's framing for the ledger: the 1.09 ns alternative was never real
— it was N divergent hand-rolls with an order-correctness bug; ~5 ns
buys one idiom, one contract, one mechanism, forever.

## Your follow-up (as your task defined it)

After the user publishes 2.2.0: bump Invar to `ivue@^2.2.0`, then the
mechanical sweep — delete each `Object.defineProperty(this, …)` block,
keep the computation body, delete the `cache()` / `cachedSet()`
helpers. Acceptance: `grep -rn "Object.defineProperty(this" src`
returns zero + full merge gate. Note the public-delegate pattern
(`static get atRest() { return this.$atRest; }`) needs no change.

## A finding for YOUR contracts — method binding has the same hole, one topology over

Your elimination #1 generalizes: `Static()`'s lazy METHOD binding
still materializes a bound function as an own data property on the
receiving class (`defineProperty(this, key, …)`). If a consumer
extends the WRAPPED `Class` (not `$Class`) and the parent's method is
read before the child's, the child's chain lookup finds the parent's
own data property — a method bound to the parent — and any `this`-
dispatched statics the child overrides are ignored, order-dependently.

Invar is safe today because the standard says children extend
`$Class`. But that safety is convention, and your house rule is that
conventions this load-bearing get recorded or mechanized. Options,
your call: (a) record "extend `$Class`, never `Class`" as an invariant
with a conventions-gate check, or (b) file a task for ivue to move
method binding to the same hasOwn-guarded shape (small perf note: that
adds the ~5 ns guard to every warm method read, which unlike
`$`-getters CAN sit in hot paths — so (a) may be the better trade).
Evidence and measurement style per your own protocol.

214	  `Static()` construction. This can make override precedence explicit, but is
215	  a larger change and increases setup work.

218	descriptor resolution, and add both read orders as regression tests. Stable
219	binding must not change native override dispatch based on which class was read

**Release title:** `ivue@2.2.1 — field fixes: order-correct method binding, $ means stable identity`

````markdown
Same-day fixes from field evidence against 2.2.0, reported by the
first production consumer.

### Fixed

- **Static method binding was order-dependent.** The bound function
  was installed as an own named property on the receiving class, so a
  parent-first read planted a parent-bound method where every
  descendant's chain lookup would find it — subclass overrides of
  `this`-dispatched members were silently ignored depending on read
  order. Methods now cache their bound function under a per-receiver
  symbol own-property (the same discipline as `$`-caches): each class
  binds itself on its own first read, in any order. Extending the
  wrapped `Class` is now safe by construction.

### Changed

- **`$`-cached values are no longer frozen.** Field evidence showed
  the shallow freeze forbade the one mutation shape it could see
  (plain-object writes — crashing a real app's boot) while allowing
  every collection mutation (`Map.set` and kin) — partial protection
  that misleads. The contract is now stated plainly: the `$` prefix
  promises **stable identity per receiver, nothing more**; whether the
  cached value is immutable config or a deliberately mutable memo
  table is the author's design.

  reactivity and static `$`-caches publishes
  `Class = Static(Reactive($Class))` — both contracts verified to
  hold through the composed class. `$` semantics are granted by the
  transform, on both the instance and static sides.

188 tests at 100% coverage on every metric, including both read
orders of the binding fix. Core entry 1,112 B gzipped, `ivue/extras`
````

Worth savoring what just happened procedurally: an agent fleet consumed a library, probed the published artifact, filed a maintainer-grade defect report with a mutation census, and the fix shipped same-day with their evidence quoted in the contract. The flywheel isn't just turning — it's peer-reviewing.
Turn took 6m 18s
is it possible to rebind the $cached getter to the cachedKey defineProperty on cached getter $ but do it using hasOwn that way we skip 5ns tax altogether?

Structurally no — and it's worth walking the exact mechanism, because the idea *sounds* like it should work and the reason it can't is the deepest fact in this whole design.

The proposal: on first read through receiver `R`, use the hasOwn logic once, then `defineProperty(R, '$atRest', { value })` — a named data property — so every later read through `R` is a raw 1.1 ns property load. Guard once, pay never.

Here's where it dies. Property lookup and your guard live in different layers:

```
DottedRender.$atRest
  → own check on DottedRender…  none
  → walk to Render…             OWN DATA PROPERTY found (planted by Render's first read)
  → return it.                  ❌ the accessor never executes
```

The `hasOwn` guard is *inside the getter* — but once any ancestor holds an own **named** data property, descendants' lookups terminate at that data property and **the getter is never invoked for them**. There is no code of ours running at that moment; there's nothing to check `hasOwn` *from*. The name is a shared channel down the inheritance chain, and an own value under the name on an ancestor silences the accessor for the entire subtree below it. That's why the task's elimination #3 was stated as an absolute: *"No arrangement of data properties can be order-correct: an own property on the parent shadows the chain for every descendant, full stop. Order-correctness structurally requires a per-read receiver check."* The symbol key is what makes the per-read check *possible* — it keeps the name resolving to the accessor forever, so our code runs on every read and can ask "whose read is this?"

I also stress-tested the escape routes before answering, and they all close:

- *Plant the named property only on subclasses, keep the wrapped class pristine?* The wrapped class **is** a receiver (it's the namespace `Class`), and any subclass's own named property would shadow *its* descendants in turn. Same hole, one level down.
- *Put the accessor on a hidden intermediate class no one uses as a receiver?* Doesn't matter — receivers form a chain **among themselves**; any receiver's own named value shadows its children regardless of where the accessor lives.
- *Detect "this class has no subclasses" and self-replace safely?* JavaScript has no subclass-creation hook — `class X extends Y` evaluates without notifying `Y`. Unknowable, forever.

So the 5 ns is not an implementation tax we haven't optimized away — it is the **price of order-correctness itself**, and `Object.hasOwn` on a symbol is already the cheapest possible form of it (no chain walk, monomorphic inline cache, one branch).

And for the case where even 6.3 ns matters, the zero-cost path already exists and is *better* than any engine trick because it's explicit at the call site — the same hoisting doctrine as hot ref reads:

```ts
const atRest = ScrollMomentum.Class.$atRest; // one guarded read
for (const row of million) {
  settle(row, atRest); // 0 ns forever after
}
```

That's the honest frame: per-read, the guard costs 5 ns; per-*algorithm*, it costs one hoist line. Meanwhile the alternative shape costs silent wrong answers in subclass topologies — which is exactly the bug class 2.2.1 just fixed in methods. We measured what correctness costs, it's five nanoseconds, and I'd sign that contract every time.

# The Namespace Pattern, Crystallized

::: warning Current exploration
This page extracts an invariant used by ivue and explores its application
outside Vue. It is research material, not part of ivue's required operating
manual.
:::

> A dependency needs a canonical address and a moment of resolution. It needs
> a container only when the answer varies by runtime context.

The namespace pattern begins below ivue. It does not require Vue, refs,
`Reactive()`, or even TypeScript namespace syntax. Its invariant is:

```text
canonical object + mutable Class slot + late dependency read
```

Each part has one responsibility:

- The canonical object names the capability.
- `Class` selects its current implementation.
- A getter or method reads dependencies after module initialization.

231	export namespace Orders {
232	  export const $Class = $Order;
233	  export let Class = $Class;
234	  export type Instance = InstanceType<typeof Class>;
235	}
236	```

238	The dot in `Orders.Class` does not create lateness. The
239	`relationMappings` getter does. Objection calls the getter after module

243	This follows Objection's native contract: `relationMappings` may be an object,
244	function, or getter, and `modelClass` may be a model constructor or module

257	### Why a getter sometimes appeared insufficient
258	
259	A static import always begins loading its target module. Under CommonJS it
260	becomes a top-level `require()`. The relation getter postpones the imported
261	value read, but it does not postpone execution of the target module.
262	
263	Path-valued `modelClass`, a thunk containing `require()`, or a `lazyImport()`
264	inside the getter adds a second kind of lateness by postponing module loading:
265	
266	| Relation form | Target module loads | Class value reads |
267	|---|---|---|
268	| Static field with imported class | during initialization | during initialization |
269	| Getter with imported class | during module-graph loading | when Objection reads the getter |
270	| Getter with path, thunk, or `lazyImport()` | when the relation resolves | when the relation resolves |
271	| Getter with `Related.Class` | during module-graph loading | when Objection reads the getter |
272	
273	The namespace form does not need to postpone module loading. Its portability
274	comes from the export shape:
275	
276	```ts
277	export namespace Orders {
278	  export const $Class = $Order;
279	  export let Class = $Class;
280	}
281	```
282	
283	Under CommonJS, a named-import transform retains the module's exports object;
284	the later getter reaches its completed `Orders.Class` property. Under ESM,
285	`Orders` is a live exported binding and the later getter reaches the same
286	selected property. The namespace is therefore one stable exported address in
287	both module systems. ESM is not required.
288	
289	What must remain late is the **read**, not the export. Do not copy the selected
290	class into another module-level binding or default export:
291	
292	```ts
293	const OrderClass = Orders.Class; // eager snapshot — loses the invariant
294	export default Orders.Class; // eager snapshot — loses later selection
295	```
296	
297	CommonJS may temporarily expose a partially initialized exports object during
298	a cycle, while ESM may leave an exported binding uninitialized during module
299	evaluation. Neither is a problem when no participant reads the namespace until
300	the relation getter runs. This works when the invariant covers the entire
301	cycle: no participant reads another participant's value while the graph is
302	loading.
303	
304	A native Node ESM project uses emitted extensions in relative specifiers, such
305	as `./Order.model.js` under `moduleResolution: "NodeNext"`, but that is a module
306	configuration detail rather than the source of the circularity guarantee.

313	- Every relation map that reads another model is a getter or method.
314	- Every `modelClass` reads `Related.Class` inside that late body.
315	- No module snapshots `Related.Class` into a top-level binding or export.

460	  export let Class = Reactive($Class); // reactive — you `new` this

468	## Provider choice and lifetime remain separate
469	
470	Static capability classes have no instance lifetime. Stateful classes still
471	need an explicit owner and remain ordinary instance classes:
472	
473	```ts
474	class $Application {
475	  readonly worker = new OrderWorker.Class();
476	}
477	```
478	
479	The `Class` slot answers which constructor is selected. The owner answers how
480	many instances exist, how long they live, and who disposes them. Keeping those
481	questions separate prevents a provider-selection pattern from becoming an
482	implicit lifetime container.
483	
484	## Boundaries remain explicit
485	
486	Late reads remove accidental initialization order. They do not make a
487	structural contradiction valid:
488	
489	- `A extends B` and `B extends A` cannot both establish a parent first.
490	- Constructors that recursively construct each other still recurse forever.
491	- A top-level `Other.Class` snapshot remains eager.
492	- A static field initialized from `Other.Class` snapshots the provider.
493	- Decorators and module side effects may still read dependencies too early.
494	- A method detached from raw `$Class` still loses static `this`; retained
495	  callbacks use the selected `Static()` class.
496	- A selected static callback remains attached to one class generation; it does
497	  not follow a later `Class` assignment.
498	
499	These are eager edges or genuine logical recursion. The pattern removes hidden
500	load-order discipline without hiding impossible graphs behind a container.
501	
502	## One invariant across runtimes
503	
504	The shared class grammar allows each runtime to add only its required adapter:
505	
506	```text
507	canonical namespace object + mutable Class slot + late reads
508	├── Node: Static() capability classes and process restart
509	├── stateful Node: ordinary instances with explicit owners
510	├── ivue: Reactive() and Vue-facing Instance typing
511	├── plugins: boot-time class composition
512	└── development: reconstruction by the existing runtime owner
513	```
514	
515	The namespace is not an ivue convention exported to Node. ivue and Node are
516	different expressions generated from the same smaller invariant.

7	# Static Classes for Node
8	
9	::: warning Current exploration
10	This page applies the namespace invariant outside Vue. The implementation is

13	
14	> Solve circularity, passable methods, and inheritance. Let the Node process

16	
17	Most backend modules are function bags. A static capability class preserves
18	that allocation-free shape while adding native inheritance and `super`. The
19	namespace supplies a late provider address. `Static()` adds one missing
20	property: a static method remains correct when a router, queue, or event
21	emitter retains it as a callback.
22	
23	## The complete scope
24	
25	| Included | Owned elsewhere |
26	|---|---|
27	| Circular-import safety through late reads | File watching and process restart |

187	## Deliberate boundaries
188	
189	### Static privacy
190	
191	Use TypeScript `private static` for class-internal data that a method reads
192	through polymorphic `this`:
193	
194	```ts
195	class $Orders {
196	  private static sequence = 0;
197	
198	  static nextId() {
199	    return ++this.sequence;
200	  }
201	}
202	
203	export namespace Orders {
204	  export const $Class = $Orders;
205	  export let Class = Static($Class);
206	}
207	```
208	
209	TypeScript `private` is an authoring-time access rule. At runtime the member is
210	an ordinary inherited property, so `Orders.Class.nextId()` works with the
211	selected subclass. Use `protected static` instead when subclasses or plugins
212	must access the member directly.
213	
214	Use a module-scoped variable or function when privacy must also hold at
215	runtime. Static capability classes primarily hold behavior, so module scope or
216	the composition root is usually the clearest owner for private capability
217	data.
218	
219	Native static `#private` has a narrower role. A selected class is a subclass of
220	`$Class`, while a native private member brands only its declaring class. A
221	method that evaluates `this.#privateMember` therefore rejects the selected
222	subclass receiver:
223	
224	```ts
225	class $Orders {
226	  static #sequence = 0;
227	
228	  static nextId() {
229	    return ++this.#sequence; // incompatible with subclass selection
230	  }
231	}
232	```
233	
234	This is native JavaScript inheritance behavior, not something `Static()`
235	should disguise. Native static private state remains valid when the method
236	accesses its declaring class lexically:
237	
238	```ts
239	class $Orders {
240	  static #sequence = 0;
241	
242	  static nextId() {
243	    return ++$Orders.#sequence; // valid, deliberately non-polymorphic
244	  }
245	}
246	```
247	
248	The standard is: avoid `this.#member` in static capability classes. Use
249	TypeScript `private` for polymorphic class encapsulation, `protected` for
250	extension points, and module scope for runtime-private state. Instance
251	`#private` fields are unaffected.
252	
253	### Stateful objects
254	
255	Sessions, actors, streams, and resource-owning workers have identity and
256	lifetime. They remain ordinary instance classes with explicit owners. A static
257	capability transform is not an instance container.
258	
259	ORM model classes such as Objection models also represent stateful instances
260	and participate in a framework-owned static protocol. They may use the
261	namespace and late `Related.Class` reads to remove relation circularity, but
262	their selected slot remains `let Class = $Class`; do not pass them through
263	`Static()`. The [Objection model pattern](/guide/namespace-pattern?experiment=1#objection-models-use-the-namespace-without-static)
264	shows the complete form.
265	
266	### Contextual providers
267	
268	One mutable namespace slot represents one application-wide selection. If a
269	provider varies by request, tenant, or session, pass that context explicitly or
270	use scoped DI.
271	
272	### Live replacement
273	
274	Lazy binding makes a callback safe; it intentionally fixes that callback to
275	one selected class. Following future `Class` assignments requires either a
276	forwarding closure on every call or owner reconstruction. This experiment uses
277	owner reconstruction through normal Node restart.
278	
279	## The resulting backend grammar
280	
281	```text
282	one module capability
283	→ one raw static class
284	→ one canonical namespace
285	→ dependencies read through getters
286	→ one selected Static() class
287	→ ordinary callbacks
288	```
289	
290	The [Namespace Pattern](/guide/namespace-pattern?experiment=1) defines the
291	smaller invariant. [Node Development by Restart](/guide/node-class-hmr?experiment=1)
292	explains why this experiment stops before inventing a hot-module runtime.

## The backend: Node capability classes

Nothing above is Vue-specific — `Static()` imports no Vue and runs
anywhere JavaScript does. On a Node backend, where most modules are
function bags, the same shape becomes the default module grammar. Two
additions complete it.

**Dependency getters read the live slot.** A capability reaches
another capability through a static getter, so the cross-module read
happens when behavior runs — never while the module graph is
initializing. Imports may be circular; nothing reads eagerly:

```ts
class $Orders {
  static get Users() {
    return Users.Class; // late — and always the SELECTED class
  }

  static submit(request: OrderRequest) {
    return this.Users.find(request.params.userId);
  }
}
```

**Retained callbacks are safe — and belong to one generation.**
Because methods bind lazily with stable identity, direct registration
works:

```ts
router.post('/orders', Orders.Class.submit);
```

The router receives one stable function whose `this` is the class
selected *at registration time*. A later `Class` assignment does not
rewrite a callback already stored inside the router — so boot
composition finishes before callbacks escape:

```text
load modules → compose raw classes → select each Static() class
→ register retained callbacks → listen
```

`Class` is mutable as a **composition slot**, not a runtime feature
flag: a kernel starts from `$Class`, applies extensions, and calls
`Static()` once on the composed result. Changing the plugin set
restarts the process and produces a new sealed generation — why the
pattern deliberately stops before a custom reload runtime is
[Node Development by Restart](/guide/node-class-hmr?experiment=1).

**One privacy rule.** Avoid `this.#member` in static capability
classes: native static `#private` brands only its declaring class, and
the selected class is a subclass, so polymorphic access rejects it.
Use TypeScript `private static` for polymorphic encapsulation
(an authoring-time rule — the selected subclass dispatches fine),
`protected static` for extension points, and module scope for state
that must be private at runtime.

One boundary carries over unchanged: a namespace slot is **one
application-wide answer**. When a provider varies by request, tenant,
or session, pass that context explicitly or use scoped DI — the
pattern replaces the container for global selection only.
